profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a large software company for a proposal called 'ReviewPilot,' which adapts the BitsAI-CR pattern to automate code review on the company's GitHub Enterprise monorepo, starting with Go services. The context is that the ML platform team has already built a RuleChecker plus ReviewFilter prototype and now wants approval for a six-week pilot on three backend teams. The agenda is to review whether the proposal is ready for pilot rollout, whether the Go rule baseline and evaluation plan are adequate, and how the feedback data flywheel will be wired into existing review workflows. The expected outcome is a decision on design approval with a short list of follow-up changes before pilot launch.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.role: Staff ML Engineer, Code Intelligence Platform
members.expertise: LLM-assisted developer tools, ranking/filtering systems, offline evaluation for code intelligence products
members.background: Priya leads the team building internal AI assistance for engineering workflows and authored the current proposal for RuleChecker plus ReviewFilter integration into pull requests.
members.private_state: Priya wants the design approved quickly so her team can start gathering real usage data this quarter; she is especially trying to avoid the pilot being blocked by additional integration asks that her team cannot staff immediately.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'Outdated Rate,' they mean the comment-level metric computed from bot comments across patchsets before merge, because that is how her team instrumented the prototype.
The 'Go baseline' is the existing internal RuleChecker package of common Go review rules, since that is the artifact her team can actually deploy first.
A system is 'pilot-ready' once model quality and safety are acceptable; operational niceties like polished UX, team controls, and richer dashboards can mature during the pilot.
The first version of the feedback flywheel should use the smallest reliable explicit signals, mainly reactions and resolution outcomes on bot-posted comments, before expanding to noisier review data.

members.name: Lucas Chen
members.role: Principal Developer Experience Engineer, Source Control & Review Infrastructure
members.expertise: Code review workflow integration, GitHub Enterprise tooling, developer-facing rollout and observability
members.background: Lucas owns the internal pull-request experience, including review bots, branch protections, and analytics that platform teams use to roll out new review automation features.
members.private_state: Lucas wants to approve the concept but needs the pilot to fit smoothly into the existing review ecosystem so his team does not inherit noisy support issues or misreported adoption metrics from a rushed launch.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss 'Outdated Rate,' they mean the merged-PR outcome metric used in DevEx reporting, because leadership cares about whether the final code changed, not patchset-level bot behavior.
The 'Go baseline' refers to the taxonomy of accepted human review issue categories compiled last quarter for reporting and governance, since that is what prior rollout discussions used.
A 'pilot' means normal in-product exposure for real teams, so readiness includes rendering, deduplication, controls, and documentation rather than only offline model performance.

If a feedback flywheel is being built, it should harvest all review signals already present in the workflow, including edited human follow-up comments and data from shadowed suggestions, not only direct bot reactions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss tracking 'Outdated Rate' during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a comment-level metric over bot-posted comments where a suggestion becomes outdated when later patchsets change the referenced code without clearly adopting the suggestion, measured during PR iteration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a merged-PR outcome metric where a suggestion is outdated only if the issue is absent from the final merged diff, regardless of patchset churn, measured after merge for reporting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term comes from the BitsAI-CR framing and sounds standardized, so both treat it as already-defined jargon; the disagreement lives in denominator, time window, and aggregation details that usually sit inside analytics specs rather than design-review conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'Go baseline' the proposal starts from
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to starting from 'the Go baseline we used last quarter.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the deployable internal RuleChecker package containing roughly 31 common Go review rules already maintained by her team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the Q4 spreadsheet taxonomy of 12 high-adoption Go review issue categories distilled from human reviewer comments in the payments org.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are real, both are colloquially called the Go baseline in adjacent meetings, and either one plausibly sounds like the obvious starting point, so neither participant feels a need to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design should be 'pilot-ready' after a few final checks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks pilot-ready means offline precision is above target, major security/privacy concerns are cleared, and basic PR posting works; dedupe polish, controls, and team-specific tuning can continue during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks pilot-ready means the end-to-end review experience is operationally complete for real teams, including GitHub rendering, deduplication with existing tools, opt-out controls, and support documentation in addition to acceptable model quality.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'pilot-ready' sounds like a shared organizational milestone, but each role naturally fills in different readiness criteria from habit; because neither side rejects the pilot in principle, the divergence feels like ordinary shorthand rather than disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: How the feedback flywheel will be wired
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'feed reviewer feedback into the flywheel.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to ingest explicit signals attached to bot-posted comments, mainly thumbs-up/down reactions and whether the referenced code changed afterward, because these are clean labels that her team can implement quickly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the system will also ingest reviewer-edited replacement comments, human resolutions linked to the same issue, and shadow-mode suggestion outcomes, because those signals already exist in the review workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the high-level goal of using feedback for continuous improvement, and the exact capture path sounds like a downstream implementation detail; both assume the obvious available signals will naturally be included.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved today with only lightweight follow-ups. The core is straightforward: take our RuleChecker plus ReviewFilter prototype, post review comments into GitHub PRs for Go services, and use the pilot to get real usage data this quarter. If this turns into a broad integration program, we're stuck. Keep it focused on the six-week pilot, three backend teams, acceptable quality and safety, and basic posting.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. I'll keep this tight. The proposal is to adapt the BitsAI-CR pattern into our GitHub review flow for Go services by combining RuleChecker with ReviewFilter, then run a six-week pilot on three backend teams. What I'm looking for today is design approval so we can move from prototype evaluation into a limited real-world rollout.

turns.inner_thought: Conceptually I'm on board, but if this shows up in normal PR flow, it has to behave like a real product surface. My team will absorb the support burden if comments render oddly, metrics don't line up, or teams can't control exposure. I want to verify we're starting from the Go baseline we used last quarter, that rollout hooks match existing review infrastructure, and that 'pilot-ready' means operationally ready, not just model-ready.
turns.utterance: From my side, the concept makes sense. The main things I want to pressure-test are whether we're starting from the Go baseline we used last quarter, whether the rollout mechanics fit the existing review path, and whether the evaluation plan is solid enough to call this pilot-ready.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's aligned on starting from the RuleChecker Go package. That's exactly what we can deploy first. And for pilot-ready, I just need him to accept that once offline precision clears target and privacy/security checks are done, we can start. We do not have bandwidth right now for perfect dedupe, controls, and rich dashboards before launch.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's the plan. RuleChecker starts from the Go baseline we used last quarter, and ReviewFilter is there to keep the quality bar where we want it. Assuming offline precision lands in the target band and the final checks clear, I think the design is pilot-ready.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, good, sounds like they're grounding in the same Go taxonomy we've referenced in prior rollout reviews. I still need to make sure reporting won't be weird. Leadership is going to look at adoption and outcome metrics in the DevEx dashboards, so Outdated Rate needs to line up with the merged-PR reporting definition teams already know.
turns.utterance: That all sounds reasonable. One thing I do want to pin down is how we'll track Outdated Rate on the pilot repos, mostly so the rollout dashboard matches what teams expect to see.

turns.inner_thought: Easy question. We already instrumented Outdated Rate on bot comments across patchsets, so we can show whether suggestions get adopted as the PR evolves. That's the practical metric for this pilot because it gives fast feedback before merge. No need to get into deeper analytics specs unless asked.
turns.utterance: The idea is that Outdated Rate gives us a read on whether comments are actually getting adopted as the review moves forward. We'll track that on the pilot repos by watching bot comments over the life of active pull requests.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, as long as the user experience feels like any other review tool in GitHub and not a rough experiment. For me, pilot-ready still includes rendering, dedupe with existing automation, some basic controls, and enough documentation that teams know what they're seeing. If those are in place, three teams is contained enough.
turns.utterance: Got it. As long as the PR experience behaves like a normal review tool, I'm comfortable starting with a limited pilot on three teams.

turns.inner_thought: He seems fine with basic posting, which is what I needed. We can smooth over UX during the pilot while collecting the first explicit feedback signals. The important thing is not to let polish work become a gate. Once comments are posting and quality is acceptable, we should start learning.
turns.utterance: That should be fine. Once the basic posting path is working, I think any remaining UX polish can continue during the pilot while feedback starts flowing into the flywheel.

turns.inner_thought: Good, and obviously the flywheel should use the review data we already have, not just the narrow bot-thread reactions. We already capture reactions, comment edits, and related thread activity in the workflow. If we're going to run a pilot in-product, we shouldn't leave easy signal on the floor.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And on the flywheel, I'd strongly prefer we reuse reviewer reactions plus edited follow-up comments so the pilot doesn't waste signal that's already present in review threads.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep scope tight here. We'll start with explicit feedback on bot-posted comments only—reactions and resolution outcomes are the clean labels we can trust and ship quickly. I can acknowledge the broader direction without committing to ingest all the messy workflow data now. Also worth reinforcing that the deployable Go package can grow after launch.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. For the initial pass, the flywheel will begin with reviewer feedback on posted bot comments, and then we can broaden from there. Similarly, the Go baseline we used last quarter gives us a clean starting point, and we can absorb more rules after the first month if the pilot data supports it.

turns.inner_thought: This is close enough to approve. I still want visibility into the baseline and the Outdated Rate dashboards before launch, because if those are aligned with the reporting and rollout views my team already maintains, support load stays manageable. I'm assuming pilot-ready includes the normal operational pieces, and it sounds like we're nearly there.
turns.utterance: Okay, then I think I'm comfortable approving the design pending a quick pass on the baseline and Outdated Rate dashboards. If we have those in place, this should stay manageable for the rollout teams.
